title: Our Zen Ancestors and Koans
speaker: Chikyo Ewan Magie
summary: Chikyo Ewan Magie takes up the Zen ancestors and the koan tradition, starting with Bodhidharma's curt reply to Emperor Wu in the Blue Cliff Record and Huineng pounding rice for nine months after hearing the Diamond Sutra. Chikyo draws on Mazu's "Ordinary mind is the way" and on Thich Nhat Hanh, whose years of statelessness pushed him toward deeper practice. A central story is Deshan's encounter with the dumpling seller, who asks which mind is eating, followed by Case 28 of the Gateless Gate, where Longtan blows out the candle. Chikyo closes with Fayan Wenyi, who answers "I don't know" when asked why he is on pilgrimage and hears that not knowing is most intimate.

sentences.text: A warm welcome, good morning, and a warm welcome to the Red Cedar Zen Life Sunday event.
I'd be very happy that you could make it today.
The dharma talk today will be given by Chikyo Yuen McGee, who comes to us all the way from Colorado.
Yuen is a long-time Seattle Soto Zen practitioner.
He ordained in 2019 with Nomon Tim Burnett here in Bellingham, and currently he is practicing with, sorry, I need to, Jodo Cliff Clusen at the Prairie Mountain Zen Center in Longmont, Colorado.
Thank you very much, Yuen, for giving another talk.
Your first one set the bar rather high, so thank you very much for taking the time to do this again.
Thank you, Chris.
Are we going to do the opening chant?

*An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma, is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas, having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good morning, everyone.
Can you hear me okay?
Yeah, thumbs up.
Okay, thank you very much.
It's lovely to see everyone and to be here with you all at Red Cedar, even though I'm streaming to you live from the Northeastern Colorado Prairie in the town of Brush.
And thank you to Judo Chris for inviting me to give the talk today and for Nomon Tim supporting all of our practice here at Red Cedar.
This talk is on koans and ancestors.
It was first given a few weeks back because we were introducing our fall class here at Prairie Mountain Zen Center, and we thought it would be a good idea to introduce the topic with a talk.
That's the Genesis.
When we come to Zen practice, we often carry ideas or images in our heads: rows of monks robed in black, sitting in stillness and silence.
Entering the zendo for the first time, we may wonder at the quiet, the lack of verbal instruction, the sense that something is happening, but we aren't exactly sure what.
Sticking around a while, we are gradually exposed to various ancestors, as well as the famous Zen stories or koans.
Yet we may wonder what these old figures and stories have to do with us or our practice.
Mystery shrouds koans and ancestors, partly due to style and cryptic concision.
It is helpful to remember that Chinese Chan monks were immersed within an intensely poetic culture, and they were well educated before they came to the monastery.
Even so, koans and koan practice are profoundly challenging, as exemplified by the stories themselves, when frequently a monk or a student misses the lesson, leaving us to puzzle it out.
This sense of mysterious puzzle permeates koans and koan practice, enhancing difficulty and anxiety.

In many ways, this is deliberate, a highly structured methodology in Zen practice that compels students to confront the koan through short phrases and through constant concentration, to eventually awaken into an appropriate response.

At the same time, Zen students meet the ancestors, including Gautama Buddha himself, first patriarch Bodhidharma, sixth ancestor Huineng, and a host of other ancestors whose journeys of awakening and practice challenge and encourage us along the way.
One classic Zen expression states, "If you meet the Buddha on the road, kill him."
This statement attempts to orient the student practitioner towards Buddha nature within; externalizing Buddha misses the mark.
As the story of Xuefeng's awakening illustrates:
*Don't you know?
What comes in through the front gate isn't the family treasure.
If you want to express the great teaching, it must flow out from your breast.
At brother Yantou's words, Xuefeng awakened at last.
Together they danced on the mountain pass, and the snow swirled and fell.*
Modern Zen students and practitioners are no different, feeling puzzled, as if they were falling short.
This sense of doubt or lack can feel pervasive, even corrosive, as if our practice was somehow insufficient, as if we ourselves are deeply inadequate or unworthy.
The ancestors can seem so deeply profound and realized that a perception of difference arises within us, a gap between seeming self and other.
Perhaps the biggest gap manifests between Buddha and ourselves.
Yet the instruction from later Mahayana Buddhism states that we are all endowed with intrinsic Buddha nature.
*It is never apart from one, right where one is,* writes Eihei Dogen.
At the same time, however, we may not feel our intrinsic Buddha nature, may feel very distant from realization, liberation, awakening, and enlightenment.
This tension runs through each devoted practitioner and frequently drives Zen students to develop and deepen their right effort, a powerful determination to wake up and realize the Buddha way.
So it is helpful to remember Buddha himself was dissatisfied with his life, despite being raised in a protected atmosphere, in a royal palace, an inheritor of privilege and prosperity.
Yet like so many of us, he felt this dissatisfaction so keenly he left the nest and began earnest exploration in the wider world.
In this respect, our own dissatisfaction can manifest as a spur, sparking us onwards in spiritual exploration.
At the same time, it's not so easy to relax into our dukkha, accept the suffering that comes to us, even as we aim to orient ourselves to [unclear: "more stride"] and more deeply committed practice.

This is the stage when Buddha encounters the four signs, three of which are experiences of profound suffering that spurred him, and the last of which was a shining bright-eyed monk who modeled the way of the spiritual journey that set in on his path.
Even so, his encounters with old age, sickness, and death opened him in such transformative ways that he set off and never turned back.
Even after Gautama sets off, we witness his great difficulties and disappointments.
His efforts at philosophical study and inquiry hit a wall.
His efforts at asceticism bring him to death's door.
He despairs.
He doesn't know which way to go.
Only after reaching this low point does Gautama recall his childhood moment of clarity sitting beneath the tree.
Somehow his great effort and inertia combine to break open consciousness and allow it to recall a moment of tranquility and sustained clarity and calm.

This recollection and tranquility leads him to experiment with what became the middle way: upright sitting in cross-legged position, breathing naturally and calmly in complete silence and stillness, allowing all things to arise within and without body, heart, and mind.
Our great Buddhist ancestors are human beings like ourselves, suffering and struggling in the wheeling world of samsara.

In some stories we see them struggle openly, while in others we meet them after enlightenment, when they have encounters with other people who suffer greed, anger, and delusion, desire, hatred, and ignorance.
Bodhidharma's encounter with Emperor Wu exemplifies this kind of story.

As the first story in a classic koan collection, Blue Cliff Record, Bodhidharma manifests as fully realized embodiment of awakened Buddha nature, yet is cryptically curt and concise in his replies to the emperor's searching questions.
He responds, "No merit, nothing holy, I don't know."
His unyielding temperament sets the tone and image of Zen for centuries.
It is an uncompromising school within which students may struggle to see their teacher as the manifestation of great Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, Bodhisattva of compassion.
Feeling deep regret, Emperor Wu starts to send an emissary to bring Bodhidharma back, but his attendant explains it is too late.
This koan can leave the student reader with regret.
We don't want to miss the lesson, and we may need to open our hearts and eye of practice to understand these strange Zen instructions and teachers as a different kind of compassionate response.
If Bodhidharma sets Zen precedent for fierce, uncompromising effort towards enlightenment, the sixth ancestor Huineng provides an every man, every person kind of image.
An illiterate woods person from the barbarian south of China, he overhears a stanza from Diamond Sutra and immediately awakens to nature of mind.
Struck by this lightning bolt, he inquires where he might learn more and is directed to the fifth ancestor Hongren's temple on the mountain.
Upon arrival, he's sent to the kitchen: pound rice, nine months.
In this story, we see the determination to awaken and coexist with our innate Buddha nature.
Just as Buddha instructs, awakening and enlightenment are not exclusive by caste, intelligence, social class, educational background.
As expressed in Dogen's Fukanzazengi: *Intelligence or lack of it do not matter.
Between the dull and sharp -witted, there is no distinction.
If you concentrate single-mindedly, that in itself is negotiating the way.
Practice realization is naturally undefiled.* Going forward in practice is a matter of everydayness.
In Platform Sutra, we meet the mystery of Huineng's early attunement to the Dharma.
It is unfathomable as to why he awakens to the Diamond Sutra's words, but he does.
Reflecting on our own stubbornness, slowness and resistance, Huineng's story illustrates humble persistence despite his challenging origins in terms of socioeconomic and educational circumstances.

Ultimately, Huineng's story exemplifies a confidence in one's intrinsic Buddha nature, the seeds of which are revealed in Buddha's own journey, where we see him with a deep, intuitive faith in his capacity to awaken.
Mazu was Huineng's Dharma grandson.
He practiced zazen relentlessly.
From Mazu's teachings and driving effort come Rinzai Zen.
Much of Zen's aura of intensity derives from the determined efforts we first see in Buddha and Bodhidharma.
It is from Mazu we learn Zen's abiding yet challenging instruction: "Ordinary mind is the way."
As with many koans and ancestor stories, the modern practitioner faces a direct statement, a declaration that seems to contradict our lived experience.
One might ask, if ordinary mind is the way, why do I suffer so much?
Or to frame it another way, if enlightenment is ordinary mind, why is my mind so chaotic, my heart so troubled, my speech and actions disordered?
Like Huineng, Mazu's teachings drew upon the Tathagata's teachings and his own awakened understanding of ordinary mind, but his method was direct and confrontational.
As Julia Janet Abels puts it in her book, Making Zen Your Own, those who came to Mazu's monastery did not receive comfort and solace.

His kicks and shouts method was designed to awaken students from delusion and ignorance of karma-driven ego mind, the habituated mind we develop through years of conditioning and immersion in the everyday world.
Yet Abels explains, Mazu did not hit or shout to punish but to awaken.
We want to believe in ourselves, have faith in ourselves, yet often are deluded about the nature of our own minds and hearts.
In times of crisis, we fall into habits of unawakened mind and suffer more.
Yet Juryu helps us see the merits of suffering and struggle.
She writes: *We awaken more profoundly out of hard times than out of the calm times in our life.

It is telling that the Chinese symbol for crisis is the same as that for opportunity.* She clarifies the deep value of this perspective and encourages its development as essential in our spiritual journey.
She says: *We as practitioners always have the opportunity to label what is happening difficult, failure, or crisis, or not to label it at all and instead see it as just this.
This view of reality without labels allows us all kinds of possibilities to arise if we could only trust the moment.
Developing such trust is the work of Zen.
It will depend on the strength of our practice and our ability to be aware when we are creating a label.
Taming and monitoring the ego mind is a primary Zen work in a crisis because a tamed mind sees the opportunities in hard times and seizes them.*
Much of the time, though, we want to push away this insight and turn aside from such hard challenging work.
We would much prefer to believe we've done enough.
Yet this is the typically deluded mind at work.
By contrast, our Buddha nature will remind us, "Delusions are endless.
I vow to end them."
Modern Zen ancestor Thich Nhat Hanh embodies this right understanding in his own determined efforts to awaken, even in the midst of the Vietnam War and his own loss of statehood and citizenship.
Due to his involvement protesting the war and presenting at the Paris Peace Talks 1968, Thay's passport was invalidated.
Applying to the French government for asylum, he became apatride, a stateless person.
While it enabled him to travel to European countries, it walled him out from Canada and the U.S. except in the case of having a proper visa.
Yet it is very difficult to apply for a visa as a stateless person.
He would be turned down as a matter of course.
This compelled him to practice even more deeply.
He says:
*My practice was the practice of mindfulness.
I tried to live in the here and now and touch the wonders of life every day.
It was thanks to this practice I survived.
The expression "I have arrived, I am home" is the embodiment of my practice.*

The suffering Thay encountered as a 40-year-old monk was profound, and while he knew a lot about Buddhism and had trained deeply, it was this excruciating exile that compelled him to awaken more completely.
In *At Home in the World*, he describes this:
*When we are deeply in touch with present moment, we can touch both past and future.
If we know how to handle present moment properly, we can heal the past.
It was precisely because I did not have a country of my own that I had the opportunity to find my true home.*
This is very important.
It was because I did not belong to any particular country that I had to make an effort to break through and find my true home.
The feeling that we are not accepted, that we do not belong anywhere and have no national identity can provoke the breakthrough necessary for us to find our true home.
Recognizing Zen ancestors past and present helps us understand practice more deeply, more fully.
"Only a Buddha and a Buddha" is the expression that unfolds from Mahakashapa's awakening on Vulture Peak when Buddha paused and raised a flower to the assembled monks.
Zen emphasizes direct wordless transmission.
It emerges out of day by day intimate practice together.
The essence of the teaching and Zen way is transmitted in this manner.
Another Zen saying goes, "When you walk in the fog, you may not notice it, but before long your robe is thoroughly soaked."
In this respect, Zen practice is completely holistic.
The deeper you go, the more thoroughly saturated you become.
In particular, body, heart, mind absorb not only teachings and ancestral stories, but attunement to ordinary mind: the keenly present, sharpened focus of being completely, wholly present.
Now, this moment.
It is because of this training that we find our true home everywhere, in every moment.
The road of practice and awakening, however, is often long.
In many ways, this is wonderful news, or it accommodates a human life, even if we seem to get a late start.
American Zen teacher Charlotte Joko Beck only began practicing in her mid-40s, yet became one of the most influential late 20th century Soto Zen teachers.
It is from her book, *Every Day Zen*, that Norman Fischer's group has its name.
Most Western practitioners are what David L.
McMahon, the scholar, calls adult converts.
In a sense, they developed within a largely Judeo-Christian culture and only turned to Buddhist practice later.
McMahon's book, *The Making of Buddhist Modernism*, reveals many complex twists and turns that continue to unfold as Zen and Buddhism migrate deeper into this culture.
It is helpful, I think, to recognize how transmission is still unfolding straight through each of us.
While it may appear like it is important to gain knowledge and special vocabulary, the story of Deshaun illustrates how knowledge is not awakening or liberation from suffering.
Deshaun was a great scholar of the Diamond Sutra.
He was also a proud intellectual, caught in habits of ego-mind, ego-centered knowing.
It was only the cunning of the dumpling lady by the side of the road that burst his bubble of pride and conventional mind.
"Reverend Monk," she asks, "what are you carrying there in your heavy pack?"
"These are my notes and lectures on the Diamond Sutra.
I am an expert.
I'm well known for my interpretation of its meaning."
"Oh, really?
Well, I will ask you a question, and if you can answer, you will get tingen for free."
"Wonderful," replied Deshaun, perhaps with a smile of satisfaction at the prospect of a free meal.
"Ask away."
"Well, Reverend Monk, in the Diamond Sutra, it says past mind cannot be grasped, present mind cannot be grasped, and future mind cannot be grasped.
Which mind are you pointing to?
Which mind is eating the tingen?"
Deshaun was thrust into silence and doubt.
He knew he could not answer.
Knew that moment.
All his scholarly knowledge fell short, far short of what the Sutra and teachings point towards.
At the roadside teahouse, he had asked the lady for tingen or something to eat.

Yet the characters in Chinese mean pointing to mind, and this old woman clearly obliged, giving Deshaun a fundamental koan that tore apart his ego-protecting confidence, plunged him into true inquiry and the real spiritual quest.
Juryu provides a concluding commentary on the story:
*The Diamond Sutra cuts through illusion of mind, yet there is no separately existing mind, no separately existing anything, but Deshaun only knew this, he had not realized it.
Like so many of us, Deshaun saw emptiness as a thing, like an object to be pondered and lectured on.
But emptiness and mind are no things.
Such truth can be seen only if ego-mind, creator of things as objects, is still.*
With the tea lady's direction, Deshaun made his way to the nearby monastery.
His own humility had been touched.
He sought deeper understanding.
Here is how the story unfolds in Case 28, Gateless Gate.
*Gateless Gate.
Deshaun visited Longshan and questioned him far into the night.
It grew late, and Longshan said, "Why don't you retire?"
Deshaun made his bows and lifted the blinds to withdraw, but was met by darkness.
Turning back, he said, "It is dark outside."
Longshan lit a paper candle and handed it to Deshaun.
Deshaun was about to take it, and Longshan blew it out.*
In one way, darkness is our blindness, our ignorance, but it is also complete non-separation, as when Chiano's bucket drops out, the moon vanishes and she awakens as the self drops away.
Deshaun's resistance is blown out.
We are left with him in the primordial dark.
In Zen, we face the wall and go into the dark.
The austerity and intensity of the practice appeal because they communicate that this is real, that this is a fundamental way.
With Xiaozhuo Kanchen, we encounter an ancestor both iconoclastic and deeply humble.
Compelled by Buddhism from a young age, he entered the monastery and ordained a novice.
Yet he sought greater depth, and he journeyed far on pilgrimage before he came upon Master Nongquan, living in seclusion on a remote mountain.
This early part of his story is instructive for us as modern practitioners.
Often our efforts to find a sangha and teacher take time and effort.
In this way, Xiaozhuo models spiritual pilgrimage before and after ordination, describes the capacity for succinct expression of Zen insight, almost unparalleled in the koan literature.
At the same time, Xiaozhuo also models longevity in the student-teacher relationship, practicing with Nongquan over 30 years after their initial meeting.
After Nongquan died, Xiaozhuo left again on a 20-year pilgrimage, settling only in a rickety, rundown, ramshackle temple he refused to upgrade.
His simplicity and humility embody Zen at its essence.
As modern Zen writer Ayya Khema puts it in her title, *Being Nobody, Going Nowhere*, Xiaozhuo lived that fundamental understanding.
Zhiyu describes the grounded nature of Xiaozhuo's enlightenment: he was content to live out the rest of his life in relative obscurity on a mountain.
He was content to [unclear: "walk the top"] and live ordinary mind at its most ordinary level.
He was content to disappear.
The mystery of our spiritual journey manifests in its unfolding, and this is why we conclude with Bayan Wenyi, who illustrates how the practice of Zen is our entire life.
Modern psychologist and Zen teacher Barry Magid makes this point another way, when he states, "Every insight is partial, requires long years of integration."
Bayan's own journey centers on pilgrimage.
Like Xiaozhuo, he wandered far and wide, as many of us do in this life.
He found companions on the way and one time emerged out of a snowstorm to take refuge in a distant monastery, going alone to face the teacher one-on-one in dokusan.
Bayan's encounter with Dijon came just at the right moment for Bayan to hear the words in the deepest way.
"Where are you going?" asked Dijon.
"Around, on pilgrimage."
"Why do you go on pilgrimage, monk?"
"I don't know."
"Ah," Dijon said, "not knowing is most intimate."
After long effort and remote journeys, we always may wonder and doubt, but Dijon helps Bayan awaken to not knowing at the heart of Zen.
Opening into unadorned freshness this moment, we see it right here, not out there at the summit of some impossibly distant peak.
Yet it may take us years, wandering like Bashou across the Shirakawa barrier into the remote north.
Entering and dwelling in the present moment is not easy.
It runs counter to conventional mind, to deeply habituated ways of thinking and understanding the world.
Even as deeply trained a teacher as Thich Nhat Hanh acknowledges how he had not yet realized practice completely.
It took heartache, exile, and loss to thrust him forward to the deeper commitment necessary to realize it fully.
Studying the ancestors and their stories is essential in Zen practice.
Yet it is only part of Zen training and cannot be solely an intellectual pursuit.

Rather, it must be combined with all the other elements, starting with zazen, incorporating sesshin or retreat practice, training in the lay temple with everyday people like ourselves, taking our training into the work world, into our families and homes, and into the monastery for residential training, and out again along that long road that leads to integration of practice at the deepest level of our being.
It is not easy, yet our liberation lies in opening to and becoming the practice of the ancestors.
*Whether we know their names or forget them when they whirl away in winter storms, what is it we have to hold onto when it is never apart from one right where one is?
From the earliest times, there have always been some who have perished along the road.
Still, I have always been drawn by windblown clouds into dreams of a lifetime of wandering.
The moon and sun are eternal travelers.
Even the years wander on.
A lifetime adrift in a boat or in old age leading a tired horse into the years.
Every day is a journey and the journey itself is home.*
Thank you.
Closing chant.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being in place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
**Participant:** Thank you so much, Huynh, for this wonderful talk.
A great way to speak about koans.
Thank you very much.
That was wonderful.
If you have any questions or comments, please unmute and speak up.
**Participant:** Thank you.
Huynh, it's great to see you and thanks for joining us today.

I really appreciate your talk and I enjoyed just all the stories about the ancestors, the things that brought them to practice and the things they encountered because I could certainly see some common ground in what brought me to practice and some of the barriers and difficulties and important lessons I have learned over the years and still have to learn.
So it was nice to just also be reminded it's a lifetime journey.
I'm curious if you'd say a little bit about the temple you're practicing with and the teacher you're practicing with in Colorado because I don't really know anything about your teacher or the temple.

He practiced zazen relentlessly. From Mazu's teachings and driving effort come Rinzai Zen. Much of Zen's aura of intensity derives from the determined efforts we first see in Buddha and Bodhidharma. It is from Mazu we learn Zen's abiding yet challenging instruction. Ordinary mind is the way. As with many koans and ancestor stories, the modern practitioner faces a direct statement, a declaration that seems to contradict our lived experience. One might ask, if ordinary mind is the way, why do I suffer so much? Or to frame it another way, if enlightenment is ordinary mind, why is my mind so chaotic, my heart so troubled, my speech and actions

disordered? Like Huineng, Mazu's teachings drew upon Takeda Togaba teachings and his own awakened understanding of ordinary mind, but his method was direct and confrontational. As Julia Janet Abels puts it in her book, Making Zen Your Own, those who came to Mazu's monastery did not receive comfort and solace. His kicks and shouts method was designed to awaken students from delusion and ignorance of karma driven ego mind. The habituated mind we develop through years of conditioning and immersion in the everyday world. Yet Abels explains, Mazu did not hit or shout to punish but to awaken. We want to believe in ourselves, have faith in ourselves,

yet often are deluded about the nature of our own minds and hearts. In times of crisis, we fall into habits of unawakened mind and suffer more. Yet Juryu helps us see the merits of suffering and struggle. She writes, we awaken more profoundly out of hard times than out of the calm times in our life. It is telling that the Chinese symbol for crisis is the same as that for opportunity. She clarifies the deep value of this perspective and encourages its development as essential in our spiritual journey. She says, we as practitioners always have the opportunity to label what is happening difficult, failure, or crisis,

or not to label it at all and instead see it as just this. This view of reality without labels allows us all kinds of possibilities to arise if we could only trust the moment. Developing such trust is the work of Zen. It will depend on the strength of our practice and our ability to be aware when we are creating a label. Taming and monitoring the ego mind is a primary Zen work in a crisis because a tamed mind sees the opportunities in hard times and seizes them. Much of the time, though, we want to push away this insight and turn aside from such hard challenging work. We would much prefer to believe we've done enough. Yet this is the typically diluted mind at work. By contrast, our Buddha nature

will remind us, delusions are endless. I vow to end them. Modern Zen ancestor Thich Nhat Hanh embodies this right understanding in his own determined efforts to awaken, even in the midst of the Vietnam War and his own loss of statehood and citizenship. Due to his involvement protesting the war and presenting at the Paris Peace Talks 1968, Thai's passport was invalidated. Applying to the French government for asylum, he became apartheid, a stateless person. While it enabled him to travel to European countries, it walled him out from Canada and the U.S. except in the case of having a proper visa. Yet it is very difficult to apply for a visa as a stateless person.

He would be turned down as a matter of course. This compelled him to practice even more deeply. He says, my practice was the practice of mindfulness. I tried to live in the here and now and touch the wonders of life every day. It was thanks to this practice I survived. The expression I have arrived, I am home, is the embodiment of my practice. The suffering Thai encountered as a 40-year-old monk was profound, and while he knew a lot about Buddhism and had trained deeply, it was this excruciating exile that compelled him to awaken more completely. In At Home in the World, he describes this, when we are deeply in touch

with present moment, we can touch both past and future. If we know how to handle present moment properly, we can heal the past. It was precisely because I did not have a country of my own that I had the opportunity to find my true home. This is very important. It was because I did not belong to any particular country that I had to make an effort to break through and find my true home. The feeling that we are not accepted, that we do not belong anywhere and have no national identity can provoke the breakthrough necessary for us to find our true home. Recognizing Zen ancestors past and present helps us understand practice more deeply, more fully. Only a Buddha and a Buddha

Another Zen saying goes, when you walk in the fog, you may not notice it, but before long your robe is thoroughly soaked. In this respect, Zen practice is completely holistic. and only turned to Buddhist practice later. It is helpful, I think, to recognize how transmission is still unfolding straight through each of us. While it may appear like it is important to gain knowledge and special vocabulary, the story of Deshaun illustrates how knowledge is not awakening or liberation from suffering. Deshaun was a great scholar of Diamond Sutra. He was also a proud intellectual, caught in habits of ego-mind, ego-centered knowing. It was only the cunning of the dumpling lady by the side of the road that burst his bubble

of pride and conventional mind. Reverend Monk, she asks, what are you carrying there in your heavy pack? These are my notes and lectures on Diamond Sutra. I am an expert. I'm well known for my interpretation of its meaning. Oh, really? Well, I will ask you a question, and if you can answer, you will get tingen for free. Wonderful, replied Deshaun, perhaps with a smile of satisfaction at the prospect of a free meal. Ask away. Well, Reverend Monk, in the Diamond Sutra, it says past mind cannot be grasped, present mind cannot be grasped, and future mind cannot be grasped. Which mind are you pointing to? Which mind is eating the tingen? Deshaun was thrust into silence and doubt. He knew he could not answer.

Knew that moment. All his scholarly knowledge fell short, far short of what the Sutra and teachings point towards. At the roadside teahouse, he had asked the lady for tingen or something to eat. Yet the characters in Chinese mean pointing to mind, and this old woman clearly obliged, giving Deshaun a fundamental koan that tore apart his ego-protecting confidence, plunged him into true inquiry and the real spiritual quest. Juryu provides a concluding commentary on the story. The Diamond Sutra cuts through illusion of mind, yet there is no separately existing mind, no separately existing anything, but Deshaun only knew this he had not realized it. Like so many of us, Deshaun saw emptiness as a thing,

like an object to be pondered and lectured on. But emptiness and mind are no things. Such truth can be seen only if ego-mind, creator of things as objects, is still. With the tea lady's direction, Deshaun made his way to the nearby monastery. His own humility had been touched. He sought deeper understanding. Here is how the story unfolds in Case 28, Gateless Gate. Gateless Gate. Deshaun visited Longshan and questioned him far into the night. It grew late, and Longshan said, Why don't you retire? Deshaun made his bows and lifted the blinds to withdraw, but was met by darkness.

Turning back, he said, It is dark outside. Longshan lit a paper candle and handed it to Deshaun. Deshaun was about to take it, and Longshan blew it out. In one way, darkness is our blindness, our ignorance, but it is also complete non-separation, as when Chiano's bucket drops out, the moon vanishes and she awakens as the self drops away. Deshaun's resistance is blown out. We are left with him in the primordial dark. In Zen, we face the wall and go into the dark. The austerity and intensity of the practice appeal because they communicate that this is real, that this is a fundamental way. With Xiaozhuo Kanchen, we encounter an ancestor both iconoclastic and deeply humble.

Compelled by Buddhism from a young age, he entered the monastery and ordained a novice. Yet he sought greater depth, and he journeyed far on pilgrimage before he came upon Master Nongquan, living in seclusion on a remote mountain. This early part of his story is instructive for us as modern practitioners. Often our efforts to find a sangha and teacher take time and effort. In this way, Xiaozhuo models spiritual pilgrimage before and after ordination, describes the capacity for succinct expression of Zen insight, almost unparalleled in the Koan literature. At the same time, Xiaozhuo also models longevity in the student-teacher relationship, practicing with Nongquan over 30 years after their initial

meeting. After Nongquan died, Xiaozhuo left again on a 20-year pilgrimage, settling only in a rickety, rundown, ramshackle temple he refused to upgrade. His simplicity and humility embody Zen at its essence. As modern Zen writer Ayya Khema puts it in her title, being nobody, going nowhere, Xiaozhuo lived that fundamental understanding. Zhiyu describes the grounded nature of Xiaozhuo's enlightenment. He was content to live out the rest of his life in relative obscurity on a mountain. He was content to walk the top and live ordinary mind at its most ordinary level. He was content to disappear. The mystery of our spiritual journey manifests in its unfolding, and this is why we conclude with

Bayan Wenyi, who illustrates how the practice of Zen is our entire life. Modern psychologist and Zen teacher Barry Magid makes this point another way, when he states, every insight is partial, requires long years of integration. Bayan's own journey centers on pilgrimage. Like Xiaozhuo, he wandered far and wide, as many of us do in this life. He found companions on the way and one time emerged out of a snowstorm to take refuge in a distant monastery, going alone to face the teacher one-on-one in Dokusan. Bayan's encounter with Dijon came just at the right moment for Bayan to hear the words in the deepest way. Where are you going, asked Dijon. Around, on pilgrimage.

Why do you go on pilgrimage, monk? I don't know. Ah, Dijon said, not knowing is most intimate. After long effort and remote journeys, we always may wonder and doubt, but Dijon helps Bayan awaken to not knowing at the heart of Zen. Opening into unadorned freshness this moment, we see it right here, not out there at the summit of some impossibly distant peak. Yet it may take us years, wandering like Bashou across the Shirakawa barrier into the remote north. Entering and dwelling in the present moment is not easy. It runs counter to conventional mind, to deeply habituated ways of thinking and understanding the world. Even as deeply trained a teacher as Thich Nhat Hanh acknowledges how he had not yet realized practice

completely. It took heartache, exile, and loss to thrust him forward to deeper commitment necessary to realize it fully. Studying the ancestors and their stories is essential in Zen practice. Yet it is only part of Zen training and cannot be solely an intellectual pursuit. Rather, it must be combined with all the other elements, starting with Zazen, incorporating Sashen or retreat practice, training in the lay temple with everyday people like ourselves, taking our training into the work world, into our families and homes, and into the monastery for residential training, and out again along that long road that leads to integration of practice at the deepest level of our being. It is not easy,

yet our liberation lies in opening to and becoming the practice of the ancestors. Whether we know their names or forget them when they whirl away in winter storms, what is it we have to hold onto when it is never apart from one right where one is?
